entries.analysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is held weakly.

It rests on something actually getting worse rather than on the absence of good news. The share of people aged 25 to 54 who are working has fallen half a percentage point over the past year, and it fell because roughly 1.44 million fewer prime-age people are employed, not because the population grew. Alongside that, employment in AI-exposed industries — information, professional and business services, finance — is down 1.27% over the year, while employment in industries AI has barely touched is up 1.27%. The exposed side is shrinking outright, not merely growing slowly.

Two limits on that, stated up front. The industry comparison covers workers in particular sectors; the employment-rate figure covers every prime-age adult in the country. Nothing here shows the people who stopped working are the ones who left exposed industries — someone who moved from a software firm to a hospital counts as a loss on one side and a gain on the other, and never touches the employment rate at all. And the entire annual decline in the employment rate happened in one quarter, between March and June. That could be survey noise that reverses. It also sits entirely after January's annual population-baseline revision, so that particular bookkeeping artifact cannot be causing the recent drop, though it may well be inflating the twelve-month figure. The level is still high: at 80.2%, the prime-age employment rate remains about a quarter point above 2019.

Nobody is being pushed out. Layoffs are at 1.1% of employment and have not moved in a year, which is normal. Hiring and quitting are both weak. That is a frozen market, not a shedding one: incumbents are safe, and the cost falls on people trying to get in or get back in. Consistent with that, the share of unemployed people who have been out of work more than six months has risen to 27.3% from 23.3% a year ago — exits are increasingly not being caught. One caution about the hiring numbers: the net difference between hiring and quitting improved slightly, but the published figures do not say which side moved. Since both rates are historically low, the likeliest reading is that quitting fell faster than hiring — workers not daring to move — which is the opposite of what the net figure superficially suggests. That is an inference, not a measurement.

The strongest thing arguing against this reading is job postings, and it is the freshest evidence available, a month ahead of everything else. Advertised openings for knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while openings for hands-on work sit about 4% above theirs — but almost all of that hole dates from the 2022 interest-rate shock and is old news. What is current is the direction: the gap has narrowed by about four points over six months and narrowed again this month. Postings normally move before employment does, so the series that should lead is pointing the other way, and it cannot be waved off as stale. What keeps it from overturning the verdict is that four points off a twenty-three point hole is small, and postings are advertised intentions rather than filled jobs.

Pay is genuinely ambiguous and is not counted for either side. Wages in exposed industries are growing 4.63% a year against 3.53% in control industries, and that gap widened four-tenths of a point in a single month — backwards from what replacement would look like. But it cannot be read at face value while exposed employment is contracting: if junior hiring has stopped, the remaining workforce skews senior and the average rises with nobody getting a raise. Economy-wide, job-changers are still doing better than job-stayers, 4.4% against 3.6%, which says movers are landing well, but that measure covers the whole economy and cannot speak to exposed industries. Productivity growth of 2.8%, up from 2.5%, is what real gains look like — though output per hour also rises when hours fall, and exposed-industry hours are falling.

The best competing explanation is the 2021-22 over-hiring unwind. Technology and professional-services firms hired far too aggressively then and have been correcting since; the exposed-versus-control employment gap was considerably worse in late 2023 than now. That correction explains most of the level of today's gap. What it explains badly is why, four years after the surge and two years past the worst of the correction, the gap has not returned toward normal but has parked in place across four straight readings, with the exposed side contracting in absolute terms. A one-off correction should have finished unwinding. That non-closing residual is the actual signal here, and it is thin.

The interest-rate story — high rates freezing hiring in rate-sensitive white-collar work, which is largely the same set of industries labelled exposed — is not fully excluded. Against it: the bond market is not pricing a downturn, and the control industries are healthy on both employment and postings, which a general shock would not permit. For it: the postings collapse dates to the 2022 tightening, not to any AI release.

Watch the prime-age employment rate chart. If it turns back up over the next few months, the market absorbed the outflow and this was a hiring wobble rather than displacement.
entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is held weakly.

Start with what it rests on, because that matters more than the label. This is not a reading built on the absence of bad news, and it is not a reading that says displacement has yet to begin. It rests on something actually getting worse: the share of Americans aged 25 to 54 who are working has fallen half a percentage point over the past twelve months, and it fell because the number of people working went down — about 1.44 million fewer prime-age people employed than a year earlier — not because the population it is measured against grew. At the same time, employment in AI-exposed industries is shrinking outright while employment in industries AI has barely touched is growing. Those two facts together are what the displacement reading is made of.

Now the honest limits, in order of how much they cost.

The first is that the two facts come from two different groups of people. The industry comparison covers workers in information, professional and business services, and finance on one side, and hands-on and in-person industries on the other. The employment-rate figure covers everyone aged 25 to 54 in the country. Nothing in the data shows that the prime-age people who stopped working are the same people who left the AI-exposed industries. A worker who moved from a software company to a hospital shows up as a loss on the exposed side and a gain on the control side, and does not show up in the employment rate at all — that person kept their job. So the inference joins two populations rather than tracking one, and that alone is enough to keep confidence low.

The second is timing. The half-point decline in the prime-age employment rate is not spread over a year. The three-month change is also half a point, meaning the entire twelve-month move happened between March and June 2026. That has two readings and both are true. One quarter of movement in a household survey with known response problems could be noise that reverses on the next print. But a decline confined to that window also sits entirely after the January 2026 population-control revision, the annual bookkeeping change that shifted the survey's population baseline down by about 1.5 million, so that particular artifact cannot be manufacturing the recent drop — while it could well be inflating the twelve-month figure. And the level is still comfortably high: at 80.2%, the prime-age employment rate is about a quarter of a point above where it stood in 2019. Nothing catastrophic has happened.

The third is that nobody is being pushed out. Layoffs are running at 1.1% of employment and have not moved in a year, which is normal. Hiring is weak, quitting is weak. That combination describes a frozen market, not a shedding one: people who have jobs are keeping them, and the cost falls on people trying to get in or get back in. Consistent with that, the share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months has climbed to 27.3% from 23.3% a year ago — exits are increasingly not being caught. A four-point rise is a large move for that share, though 27% is unremarkable by historical standards; it went past 40% after the 2008 crisis. It is the weakest of the supports here, partly because it is a ratio that also rises when short-spell unemployment falls.

One measurement problem worth naming rather than hiding: the hiring readout publishes current hiring and quitting rates and the net twelve-month change in the difference between them, but not how much each side moved. The net improved by a tenth of a point. Given that both rates are historically low, the likeliest composition is that quitting fell faster than hiring — workers not daring to move, which is not the improvement the net figure superficially reads as. That is an inference, not a measurement, and it should be treated as one.

Now the evidence against the displacement reading, which is substantial.

The strongest piece is job postings, and it is the freshest data in the run — July 2026, a month ahead of everything else. Advertised openings for knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level, while openings for hands-on work sit about 4% above theirs. That is a dramatic gap, but almost all of it dates from the 2022 interest-rate shock and is not news. What is news is the direction: the gap has narrowed by roughly four points over the past six months, and narrowed again this month. Postings usually move before employment does, so a panel that ought to lead is pointing the other way, and it cannot be dismissed as stale because it is newer than everything supporting the reading. What keeps it from flipping the verdict is that four points off a twenty-three point hole is small, and that postings are stated intentions, not filled jobs. A narrowing gap is also consistent with an adjustment that already happened and has stopped.

The second is pay. Wages in AI-exposed industries are growing at 4.63% a year against 3.53% in the control industries, and the gap widened by four-tenths of a point in a single month. On its face that is the augmentation case: employers paying more for exactly the workers AI is supposed to be replacing. But it cannot be taken at face value while exposed-industry employment is contracting. If junior hiring in those industries has stopped, the remaining workforce skews senior and the average wage rises with nobody getting a raise. A four-tenths jump in one month alongside a shrinking headcount is precisely the shape of that composition effect. The economy-wide individual wage tracker does not settle it — people who change jobs are still getting 4.4% against 3.6% for people who stay, which says movers are still landing well — but that tracker covers the whole economy and cannot speak to exposed industries specifically. So the wage panel is genuinely ambiguous, and it is not counted for either side.

Productivity growth of 2.8%, up from 2.5%, is what gains from a real technology look like in the aggregate, and that is a point for augmentation. The catch is arithmetic: output per hour also rises when hours fall, and hours in the exposed industries are falling. One quarter inside the range seen during the late-1990s internet boom is not a break in trend. Separately, and counting toward nothing: labour's share of national income is at 51.0%, down about a point over the year across four consecutive quarterly declines, and below its previous record low. Rising productivity alongside a record-low labour share is the shape you would expect if gains were flowing to capital rather than workers, but that series drifts down for reasons that long predate AI, and ordinary recessions moved it faster.

Two alternative explanations deserve to be taken seriously and neither was adopted.

The 2021-22 over-hiring unwind is the best of them. Technology and professional-services firms hired far too aggressively in 2021 and 2022 and have been correcting ever since; the exposed-versus-control employment gap was much worse in late 2023 than it is now. That correction plausibly explains most of the level of today's gap and essentially all of the 2023 trough. What it explains badly is why, four years after the hiring surge and more than two years past the worst of the correction, the gap has not returned toward normal but has parked roughly where it is, with the exposed side contracting in absolute terms rather than merely growing slowly. Four consecutive readings have it flat. A one-off inventory correction should have finished unwinding by now. That non-closing residual, with an outright contraction on the exposed side, is the thing being read here, and it is thin evidence.

The interest-rate story is the other. High rates suppress hiring in rate-sensitive white-collar work, which is largely the same set of industries labelled exposed, and the postings collapse dates to the 2022 tightening rather than to any AI product release. Two things argue against it as the whole story. The bond market is not pricing a downturn — the yield curve is positively sloped at about four-tenths of a point. And if the weakness were general, the control industries would be weak too; instead their employment is up 1.27% over the year and their job postings are above pre-pandemic levels. That test cuts in favour of the displacement reading, with one soft joint: the control industries have their own tailwinds, health-care demographics and travel normalisation among them, so their strength is not pure proof that no macro shock is present.

An immigration-enforcement story was considered and set aside. The only number supporting it is the fall in the measured prime-age population, which is the one figure most contaminated by the annual population-control revisions. And immigrant employment concentrates in construction and hospitality — the control group, which is growing — so that story predicts the opposite of the divergence actually observed.

On the technology itself: 21.7% of firms now report using AI in producing goods or services, up from 17.3% in November 2025, and 38.8% among firms with 250 or more employees, so the share of workers at an adopting employer is higher than the share of firms. That is enough deployment for a displacement reading to be physically possible. It is not evidence that displacement occurred; adoption is equally the precondition for augmentation.

The month's news did not move anything. Payrolls rose 57,000 in June with unemployment at 4.2%, which says the aggregate economy is still creating jobs, slowly — a genuine caution against this reading, though jobs created somewhere else do not establish that the people who left exposed work filled them. Coverage of Middle East conflict raises the possibility of an energy-price shock freezing hiring, but the labour figures here run only through June and May, and a broad shock would also hit the control industries, which are growing. No employer in the current news is attributing headcount reductions to AI.

What would show this reading was wrong: the prime-age employment rate turning back up. Specifically, if its twelve-month change recovers to roughly flat by late October while the long-term-unemployed share falls to 26% or below, the market absorbed the outflow and this was a hiring wobble rather than displacement. That is well within the demonstrated month-to-month range of both series, and three more monthly readings land before then. The postings spread was considered as the test instead, since it is the freshest panel and the one arguing against the verdict, but a narrowing spread is equally consistent with displacement having already happened and the flow having stopped, so it does not discriminate.

entries.analysis:
The reading is still displacement, and still weak. It rests on one thing deteriorating, not on the absence of harm: the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job has fallen half a point over the past year, to 80.2%, and the number of prime-age people actually employed is down about 1.4 million, so this is not a ratio distorted by a growing population. That is an economy-wide figure. This is not augmentation working — nothing here shows AI-exposed work expanding.

Almost nothing moved since last month. The jobs and pay comparisons, the employment decline, productivity, the labour share and the adoption figures are all unchanged. The job-ads number changed from -27.1 to -28.1, but the month it refers to did not change, so that was a revision to an already-published reading, not the gap widening. Treat this as a re-reading of a standing situation, not news.

The strongest support is that the damage is specific rather than general. Employment in AI-exposed industries is shrinking outright, down 1.3% over the year, while industries AI has barely touched added jobs at 1.3%. Job ads for knowledge-work occupations sit about 23% below their February 2020 level; ads for hands-on occupations sit about 5% above theirs. Those cover different groups of workers, which is the point: a broad slump would drag the untouched side down too, and it has not. Alongside that, 27.3% of the unemployed have now been out of work more than six months, up 4 points over the year. Layoffs are at their normal rate and unmoved, while hiring is weak. Nobody is being pushed out; firms have simply stopped replacing people, and the cost lands on those trying to get in.

The strongest argument against is that the AI-specific gaps are healing, not widening. The jobs gap between exposed and untouched industries narrowed slightly and has been flat across four readings, and it is less than half as wide as at its worst in late 2023. The job-ads gap has closed by about 2.8 points over six months, and job ads usually move first. The obvious non-AI explanation covers most of it: information and professional services over-hired in 2021 and 2022 and have been unwinding ever since, which predates today's tools. What that explanation does not cover is thin but real — we are three and a half years past that hiring peak and exposed employment is still contracting outright, not merely growing slowly, while firm adoption of AI has climbed from 17.3% in November 2025 to 21.7% now, and to 38.8% among firms with over 250 employees. A correction still running this long needs its own explanation. That residual is why this reading survives, and its thinness is why confidence is low.

Three further cautions. Job switchers are still getting paid more to move, 4.4% against 3.6% for stayers — not what a displacement episode eventually produces, though a healthy middle can hide a minority landing badly. June payrolls rose 57,000 with unemployment at 4.2%: soft, but not contraction. And the whole of the prime-age employment drop happened in the last three months, in a household survey with known response problems, from a level still slightly above 2019. Where things stand is fine; the direction is not.

Productivity growth of 2.8% is often read as the augmentation counterweight. It is not usable as one: output per hour also rises when hours fall faster than output, so labour shedding produces the same print, and this figure is a quarter older than the employment data.

What to watch: the prime-age employment-rate chart. If its twelve-month change climbs back toward flat, people are landing again and this displacement reading was wrong.
entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, held at low confidence, and it is a re-reading of a standing situation rather than a response to anything new.

Start with what this is not. It is not augmentation working. Augmentation working would look like hiring in AI-exposed work picking up, job ads for knowledge work climbing back toward where they were before the pandemic, and pay rising alongside a growing headcount. None of that is on the board. Job ads for knowledge-work occupations sit about 23% below their February 2020 level, while ads for hands-on occupations sit about 5% above theirs. Employment in AI-exposed industries is shrinking outright, down 1.3% over the past year, while industries AI has barely touched added jobs at 1.3%. Those two figures cover different groups of workers by design — that is the point of the comparison — and the contrast is what makes the shrinkage look specific rather than a general slump. A broad downturn drags the untouched industries down too, and they are not down.

What the displacement reading actually rests on is a single deterioration, and I want to be precise about which one. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job has fallen half a percentage point over the past twelve months, to 80.2%. That is an economy-wide number, not an exposed-industry one. Crucially, the decline is not an artifact of a bigger population making the ratio look worse: the number of prime-age people actually employed fell by about 1.4 million. So the people leaving are not being caught somewhere else quickly. Alongside that, the share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months is 27.3%, up 4 points over the year. That is what a market that is slow to reabsorb people looks like.

The mechanism underneath is not mass firing. Layoffs are running at their normal rate, 1.1% of employment per month, and have not budged. Hiring is weak, 3.3% of employment per month against quits of 1.9%. Weak hiring plus normal layoffs is a frozen market, not a shedding one: firms are not pushing people out, they are not replacing the ones who leave, and the cost falls on people trying to get in or get back in rather than on incumbents. That is compatible with AI quietly removing work at the entry level. It is equally compatible with a hiring freeze for any other reason. Nothing on the board settles which.

Now the case against, which is substantial, and is why this reading is weak rather than firm.

First, the AI-specific gaps are healing, not widening. The jobs gap between exposed and untouched industries has narrowed slightly over the last month and has been essentially flat across the last four readings, and it is less than half as wide as it was at its worst in late 2023. The job-ads gap has closed by about 2.8 points over six months. If postings move first, as they usually do, the exposed side is stabilising. That is the single most uncomfortable fact in this reading, and it is coming from the freshest data and from the better measure of who is actually exposed — occupations rather than whole industries, which is a real advantage, because an industry cut counts a janitor at a software firm as exposed.

Second, there is a well-established non-AI explanation for most of the shape here. Information and professional services over-hired badly in 2021 and 2022 and have been unwinding it ever since. That predates the current tools, and it plausibly accounts for most of the current jobs gap and for the initial opening of the postings gap in 2022, which was substantially about interest rates. The residual it leaves is thin but real: we are now three and a half years past the peak of that hiring bulge, exposed employment is still contracting in absolute terms rather than merely growing slowly, and firm adoption of AI has risen through the same window, from 17.3% of firms in November 2025 to 21.7% now, and to 38.8% among firms with more than 250 employees. A correction still running this long after the fact starts to need its own explanation. I do not think that residual is strong. It is one of the reasons this reading is low confidence rather than medium.

Third, people who change jobs are still landing well. Job switchers are seeing pay growth of 4.4% against 3.6% for those who stay, a premium slightly wider than its 2010s norm. In a genuine displacement episode you would eventually expect movers to land worse. The caveat runs both ways: that is a median across the whole economy, and a healthy median can sit on top of a minority of displaced knowledge workers landing badly, which is exactly the tail this measure cannot see.

Fourth, the official June jobs report was positive: payrolls up 57,000 and unemployment at 4.2%. That is soft but it is not contraction. It comes from the employer survey and covers all ages and all industries, so it does not refute the household-survey decline in prime-age employment and the household survey does not refute it either. They are different instruments measuring different things.

On pay in exposed industries, I am deliberately not using it as evidence either way. Pay in AI-heavy industries is growing at 4.6% against 3.5% in the untouched industries, and that widened noticeably this month. On its face that looks like the opposite of displacement. But employment in those same industries is falling, which means the mix of who remains is changing. If junior hiring has stopped, the surviving workforce skews senior and the average wage rises with nobody getting a raise. I checked this against the economy-wide measure of what individual workers' pay is doing, which is flat to recovering — so there is no clear individual-level confirmation of the industry acceleration, but that check cannot speak to exposed industries specifically. The composition question is unresolved, so the pay gap counts for neither side.

Productivity is the strongest single thing on the board for the augmentation story, and it does not hold up as evidence. Output per hour grew 2.8% in the first quarter of 2026, up from 2.5%, briefly inside the range the economy managed during the late-1990s internet boom. Two problems. It is economy-wide and cannot be attributed to AI-exposed work. And output per hour rises mechanically when hours fall faster than output, which means a print of this shape is also what a labour-shedding episode produces. It does not distinguish the two stories. It is also a quarter older than the jobs and employment data, so it cannot yet reflect anything recent. I flag that because it cuts against this reading: if hours have fallen further since March, the next productivity print may be higher still, and it will still not discriminate.

One descriptive figure worth noting without counting it: labour's share of national income fell to 51.0%, a new low for the series and a fourth consecutive quarterly decline, down a full point over four quarters. That is fast by historical standards, though ordinary recessions have produced faster falls. Set against productivity growth of 2.8%, it says the gains are showing up somewhere other than pay. Both are economy-wide figures and neither proves anything about AI-exposed workers.

Almost nothing moved this month. The exposed-versus-untouched jobs gap, the prime-age employment decline, the long-term unemployment share, hiring and layoffs, productivity, the labour share, the pay comparisons and the adoption figures are all unchanged from last month's readings. The job-ads spread number changed from -27.1 to -28.1, but the date attached to it did not move, so that is a revision to an already-published month rather than a new observation, and it should not be read as the gap widening. The yield curve steepened marginally and remains positively sloped, with expected inflation at 2.3%, so there is no independent recession signal to lean on in either direction.

Alternatives I considered and rejected. Reallocation rather than displacement: the test is whether the exposed-versus-untouched gap is widening while overall employment, long-term unemployment and hiring hold steady, which would mean people are moving rather than being removed. Two of those three do not hold — prime-age employment is falling in level terms and long-term unemployment is up. Against that, the untouched industries adding jobs at 1.3% is precisely what reallocation looks like from the receiving end, and no panel here follows individuals across industries, so I cannot show that the people who left exposed work are not the ones filling those jobs. That is a genuine hole. Confounded: I can name competing causes, the 2021-22 correction and the 2022 rate shock, but the data do not currently support either as the dominant explanation, since the curve is not inverted, the untouched industries are healthy on both jobs and ads, and the exposed contraction is ongoing rather than fading. Mixed evidence with a direction is not the same as confounded.

Also on the record: the war coverage in the news this month is too recent to appear in June data, and in any case a war would hit the untouched industries too — and they are the healthy side. No employer in this month's news attributed headcount cuts to AI, so there is no company claim to test against the numbers.

One caution about the employment decline itself, which is the pillar of this reading. The whole of the twelve-month drop happened in the last three months. That is one quarter of evidence, in a household survey with known response-rate problems, and the level, 80.2%, is still slightly above where it stood in 2019 — historically a strong labour market. Where things stand is fine; the direction is not. And a falling employment rate with flat layoffs is at least as consistent with people withdrawing from the labour force as with work being destroyed. This measure cannot separate those.

What would show this reading is wrong: the prime-age employment rate turning back up, with its twelve-month change improving from half a point down to roughly flat, while the jobs gap between exposed and untouched industries also narrows back inside its normal range. That would mean people are landing again. The employment-rate chart publishes monthly, so three more readings arrive before late October.

entries.analysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is a weak one. It rests on deterioration that is actually present, not on the absence of improvement: prime-age employment (ages 25 to 54) is down about 1.4 million over twelve months in the household survey, and the share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months has risen 4 points in a year, to 27.3 percent.

Nothing changed this month. Not one panel's headline number moved. This is the same picture read again, not a new development.

The strongest support is the split between industries. Employment in the industries AI touches most — information, professional services, finance — is down 1.27 percent over the year, while employment in hands-on industries like construction, health care and hospitality is up 1.27 percent. One side is shrinking outright; the other is growing healthily. A general slowdown does not spare construction and hospitality while hollowing out office work. Note, though, that this gap is not widening: it was slightly wider a quarter ago, and at its 2023 worst it was more than twice as large. The news is persistence, not acceleration. Some of it is still the unwinding of the 2021-22 over-hiring in those same industries — but four years on, that unwind leaves exposed employment falling in absolute terms rather than merely growing slower, and that residual is what this reading is built on.

The strongest thing against it is fresher than the evidence for it. Job postings move before headcount, and the postings data runs a month ahead of the employment data here. Postings for knowledge work sit 22.8 percent below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on work sit 5.3 percent above theirs — but that gap has narrowed over the past six months. Much of the level is a 2022 interest-rate event still sitting in place. A narrowing gap is not what an accelerating displacement episode produces. It is not augmentation either: that would mean knowledge-work postings climbing back toward pre-COVID levels, and being nearly a quarter below is not that.

Two further doubts. Productivity across the whole economy is growing 2.8 percent a year, up from 2.5 percent, matching the late-1990s boom — but it covers all workers, not just AI-exposed ones, it is five months old, and output per hour also rises simply when low-productivity hours are cut. And people who switch jobs are still getting bigger raises than people who stay, 4.4 percent against 3.6, which is what opportunity-driven moving looks like rather than distress.

One contradiction a reader should know about. The employer survey says the economy added 57,000 jobs in June with unemployment at 4.2 percent, while the household survey says prime-age employment is shrinking. They measure different things and neither refutes the other, but the household survey is the one with known response problems, and almost the entire twelve-month fall happened in a single quarter. If the employer survey is the truer picture, this displacement reading is wrong.

Finally, on character: layoffs are normal at 1.1 percent and flat, while hiring is weak. That is a frozen market, not one shedding people. Incumbents are not being pushed out; the burden falls on entrants and on anyone who leaves. A frozen market is also exactly what "displacement hasn't started, employers are just cautious" looks like from outside, and this data cannot fully rule that out. The level of prime-age employment also remains about a quarter of a point above 2019 — the flow has turned, the stock has not.

What to watch: the prime-age employment-rate chart. If its twelve-month change climbs back toward flat, people leaving exposed work are being reabsorbed and this displacement reading fails.
entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is a weak one. It rests on deterioration that is actually present in the data, not on the absence of improvement: the number of people aged 25 to 54 in work has fallen by about 1.4 million over twelve months in the household survey, and the share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months has climbed 4 percentage points in a year to 27.3 percent. Those are things going wrong now, not things failing to get better.

Nothing changed since the last analysis. Not one panel's headline number moved. This is the same picture read again, and the honest description of it is a configuration that has parked in a displacement-shaped position rather than a new development.

What the exposed-versus-control jobs panel says. Industries where AI can do a meaningful share of the work — information, professional and business services, finance — are shrinking, down 1.27 percent in employment over the past year. Industries where the work is physical — construction, health care, hospitality, transport — are growing at 1.27 percent. Name the moving sides rather than the gap: one side is contracting in absolute terms, the other is expanding at a healthy clip. That combination is the strongest thing in favour of an AI-specific reading, because a general economic slowdown does not politely spare construction and hospitality while it hollows out office work. It is also worth saying that this gap is not widening. It was 2.61 points a quarter ago and is 2.54 points now, a slight narrowing, and at its worst in late 2023 it was more than twice as wide. The news here is persistence, not acceleration.

The hiring correction, weighed honestly. Exposed industries hired far too aggressively in 2021 and 2022 and have been unwinding it ever since. That explains why this gap opened and explains its 2023 extreme. Four years on it plausibly still explains much of the level. What it does not explain is why exposed employment is now negative in absolute terms while the control side grows, and why the gap has not travelled back toward its 2010s norm of roughly one point. A correction that has run four years and still leaves outright contraction is doing less work than it was doing in 2023. That residual is what the displacement reading is built on, and it is modest.

What argues hardest against the displacement reading. Three things, and none of them is decorative.

First, and most seriously, the freshest panel points the other way. Job postings are the earliest thing to move when hiring changes, and the postings data runs a month ahead of the employment data supporting this reading, so it cannot be waved off as stale. Postings for knowledge work sit 22.8 percent below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on work sit 5.3 percent above theirs — a wide gap, but that gap has narrowed over the past six months, by 2.8 points. Much of the level is a 2022 interest-rate event that has simply stayed put and is not news. A narrowing spread is not what an accelerating displacement episode produces. It is not augmentation either: augmentation on this panel would look like knowledge-work postings climbing back toward their pre-COVID level, and being nearly a quarter below it is not that.

Second, productivity. Output per hour across the whole economy is growing at 2.8 percent a year, up from 2.5 percent, which is inside the range the late-1990s internet boom produced. That is what augmentation working would look like in the aggregate. Two things blunt it. It covers every worker in the country and cannot say anything about AI-exposed industries specifically. And it is five months old, three months older than the employment numbers carrying this reading, so it cannot yet reflect the recent turn. There is also a mechanical trap: output per hour rises when low-productivity hours are shed, so a displacement episode and an augmentation episode can print the same productivity number.

Third, people who change jobs are still doing well. Across the economy, job switchers are getting pay rises of 4.4 percent against 3.6 percent for people who stay put. When moving pays, people are usually moving toward opportunity rather than fleeing trouble. This is the single best argument that what is happening is reallocation rather than removal. Its limit is that it is an economy-wide median and cannot speak to exposed industries, and a collapse concentrated in a minority of workers is exactly what a median hides.

The contradiction inside the labour data, stated plainly. The employer survey says the economy added 57,000 jobs in June and unemployment is 4.2 percent. The household survey says prime-age employment fell over the year. These are different surveys of different things and neither refutes the other, but a reader trusting the prime-age number is owed the knowledge that the other main measure of employment is not corroborating it that month. The household survey is also the one with documented response-rate problems in this period, and almost the entire twelve-month fall in prime-age employment happened in a single quarter. If the employer survey is telling the truer story, this displacement reading is wrong.

Two further things that shape how the displacement should be characterised. Layoffs are running at 1.1 percent of employment and are flat — completely normal. Hiring is weak, at 3.3 percent, and quitting is weak too, at 1.9 percent. Weak hiring with normal layoffs is a frozen market, not a shedding one. Nobody is being pushed out; the cost falls on people trying to get in and on anyone who leaves. That fits the long-term-unemployment picture: exits are not being caught. But a sceptic can fairly say a frozen market is exactly what "displacement hasn't started, employers are just cautious" looks like from outside, and this data cannot fully rebut that.

Also, the stock of employment is still fine even as the flow has turned. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds in work remains about a quarter of a point above where it was in 2019. This is why the reading stays weak.

Alternatives considered and rejected. A general recession: rejected, because control industries are growing and their postings are above pre-pandemic levels, and layoffs are normal. A recession does not do that. An interest-rate-driven cut to white-collar hiring: real, and it explains the standing level of the postings gap, which opened with the 2022 tightening before current AI tools were widely deployed — but financial conditions are easing now, not tightening, so it explains a level rather than the current flow. Calling this month confounded would require naming a cause with a series in front of me showing it deteriorating, and there is none.

On the wage panel: pay in exposed industries is growing 4.63 percent against 3.53 percent in control industries, faster in the industries AI touches most. That looks like augmentation, but it cannot be used as evidence either way here, because exposed employment is falling. If entry-level hiring in those industries has stopped, the remaining workforce skews senior and the average wage rises with nobody getting a raise. Unresolved, and cited as support for nothing.

Two other numbers, recorded without being counted. AI adoption reached 21.7 percent of firms, up from 17.3 percent in November 2025, with much higher rates at large employers — this makes a displacement story possible but causes nothing on its own. And the share of national income going to workers has fallen for four straight quarters to 51.0 percent, the lowest in a series running back to 1947. Productivity rising while the labour share sets a record low means the aggregate gains are not reaching workers. It is an economy-wide number with forty years of pre-AI decline behind it, so it does not vote here, but it is the most striking figure on the board.

What would show this reading is wrong. If the prime-age employment rate's twelve-month change climbs back to roughly flat while the long-term-unemployed share falls back under 26 percent, the outflow from exposed work is being reabsorbed and the displacement reading fails. That series just moved half a point in three months, so retracing it inside a quarter is well within its demonstrated volatility.

entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is held with low confidence.

It matters what that rests on. This is not a case of saying displacement has not started and there is nothing to see; the reading rests on deterioration that has actually been observed in the data, not on the absence of good news. Two things are happening at once. Job growth in the industries most exposed to AI is negative: employment in those industries is down 1.27% over the past year, while the comparison industries AI has barely touched are adding jobs at 1.27%. And the wider labour market is not visibly catching the people leaving: the share of Americans aged 25 to 54 with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months, and the drop comes from employment falling by about 1.4 million rather than from population growth. When a specific slice of the economy is shedding work and the aggregate is not soaking it up, that is the combination that separates displacement from ordinary reshuffling.

Nothing moved this month. Of the thirteen panels, one changed, and the change was a small downward revision to a job-postings figure already published for July, not a new observation. The industry job counts, the household employment survey, the pay series, productivity, adoption and the capability benchmarks are all exactly where they were. So this month adds no evidence in either direction, and everything below is the same body of evidence read again.

The character of the exposed-industry weakness is worth spelling out, because it is not mass firing. The layoff rate is 1.1 and falling, below its own normal range. Hiring is weak at 3.4, and quits are down to 2.0. That is a frozen market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, and the cost is falling on people trying to get in and on people who have already left. A market like that can produce a falling employment share with almost nobody being fired. If AI is removing work here, it is doing it through the hiring door rather than the exit door, and that shape also explains why the long-term unemployed share has climbed to 27.3% of the jobless, up four points in a year: exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.

Now the case against, which is strong enough that it holds the confidence down to low.

The freshest evidence on the dashboard disagrees with the displacement reading. Job postings are the leading indicator here, and they are improving. Postings for exposed knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on control work sit about 5% above theirs, which looks damning until you read the direction rather than the level: the shortfall in knowledge-work postings has been closing over the past six months, not widening, and the current gap is narrower than its own average since 2023. Much of that level is a hangover from the 2022 rate shock rather than anything to do with AI. Postings data is one month newer than the industry job counts I am leaning on. So the newest thing I have argues against the verdict I have written, and I am saying so rather than burying it.

The same is true across a longer horizon. The gap between exposed and control industry job growth was far worse in late 2023 than it is now — the exposed side was contracting relative to controls by more than five points then, against two and a half now. That divergence peaked before AI tools diffused widely and has been shrinking while firm adoption rose from 17.3% of businesses last November to 21.7% now. A signal that was loudest before the tools arrived looks more like the 2021-22 over-hiring correction decaying than like an AI effect ramping up. It is also worth noting that half of the current gap is the control side being genuinely strong: if the people leaving exposed industries walked into construction, health care and hospitality, this is what benign job-switching would look like on this chart.

Pay does not behave the way displacement usually does either. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing at 4.63% a year against 3.53% in the control industries. If AI were making these workers redundant, you would expect their pay to lag, not lead. But this cannot be taken as evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time: if entry-level hiring in those industries has stopped, the people left behind skew senior and the average wage rises without anyone getting a raise. I cannot separate those two stories with what is here, which is the main reason I did not read this as augmentation. The one cross-check available is economy-wide, not exposed-specific: people who switch jobs are still getting 4.4% pay growth against 3.6% for those who stay. That premium is not collapsing, which is the single cleanest piece of evidence against the displacement reading — people are still moving jobs for opportunity rather than out of distress. It is a median across the whole workforce, so distress concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly what it would miss.

Productivity is running at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, against a pre-2020 norm closer to 1.3%. Gains are visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like, and this is the strongest thing here pointing that way. Two caveats: the figure is five months older than the labour panels, and it is economy-wide, so it cannot be attributed to AI or to exposed industries. Alongside it, labour's share of national income has fallen for four straight quarters to 51.0%, about a point over the year against a long-run drift of roughly a tenth of a point a year. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story has, though ordinary recessions have produced sharper falls in labour's share than this one.

The largest weakness in this reading is not any of the above; it is a data problem, and readers relying on the prime-age employment figure are owed it. All of the twelve-month fall in the prime-age employment share happened inside the most recent quarter — the twelve-month and three-month changes are the same half point. So this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it. Worse, the January 2026 Census population-control revision put a level shift of roughly 1.5 million into this survey, and the fall in employment I am leaning on is about 1.4 million, uncomfortably close to that. The published ratio is meant to be computed consistently within a control regime, and it fell on both the twelve-month and three-month views, which is why I have treated the revision as a fragility rather than as an outright alternative explanation. But I am not fully persuaded, and if this fall is quietly revised away rather than reversed, the displacement reading loses its load-bearing fact. The household survey's response rates also degraded through late 2025. Three of the readouts I lean on come from that same survey, so their agreement with each other is worth less than it looks.

Two further tensions I have not resolved. First, the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey at the aggregate level: payrolls rose 57,000 in June and unemployment is 4.2%. Those are economy-wide figures and cannot be used to say anything about exposed industries specifically, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the aggregate market is failing to absorb people, which is precisely the claim doing the work here. Second, if weakness is confined to exposed industries while control industries are healthy, then a falling economy-wide employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either a measurement artefact or a broad softening the control industries are not showing. That does not add up cleanly, and I would rather say so than paper over it.

On the cyclical alternative: the yield curve is not inverted, and more to the point, a general downturn would drag the control industries down with the exposed ones. It has not. Control industry jobs, pay and postings are all healthy and layoffs are low, so a plain macro contraction does not fit. The rate-sensitivity story is the one worth watching — white-collar hiring is where the 2022 rate shock landed — but if rates were again the driver, the knowledge-work postings shortfall should be widening, and it is narrowing.

Finally, several panels that get talked about a lot contribute nothing here and I have not used them. AI systems now beat or tie human experts on about 71% of tested work tasks, and win outright just under half the time; the leading model can sustain tasks of roughly three hours at the measured reliability level. A model clearing an expert on a benchmark is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert. Adoption at 21.7% of firms — with 38.8% of large employers using AI in some function against 20.8% of the smallest — establishes only that the tools are in the building in sufficient numbers for a displacement story to be possible at all. It causes nothing by itself, and the bar for counting as an adopter is low.

What would move first if this is turning: the prime-age employment share. If it climbs back to flat or better against a year earlier while the long-term unemployed share retreats, the aggregate market is catching exits again and the displacement reading was wrong. That series publishes monthly, so there will be three more observations before the end of October.

Postings lead actual hiring, this measure sorts by type of work rather than by industry, and it runs a month fresher than everything supporting the displacement reading. So the indicator that should turn first says demand for exposed work is stabilising.

entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is held with low confidence. It rests on positive evidence that things are getting worse for workers, not merely on the absence of improvement: employment among 25-to-54-year-olds is down about 1.44 million over twelve months, and the share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months has climbed 4.0 points to 27.3%. That is absorption failing, not absorption failing to improve. What keeps the confidence low is that the deterioration is one quarter old, the AI-specific jobs gap has stopped widening, and the fastest-moving indicator on the board is pointing the other way.

Nothing in the labor data moved this month. Every labor panel — jobs, employment rate, pay, postings, productivity — carries the same reading it carried last month, mostly through June 2026, with job postings through July. Three numbers on the board did change and none of them is a labor number. The share of firms using AI in any business function was restated at 21.5% for July, down from 21.5's earlier printing of 21.7% for the same month; that is a revision or a change in who answered the survey, not adoption falling. A macro-regime summary ticked down a tenth. One AI capability rating fell about fifteen points on a re-scored pool. None of these changes anything about what is happening to workers.

The exposed-versus-control jobs panel

Industries most exposed to AI — information, professional and business services — are shrinking outright, down 1.27% over the year. Industries AI has barely touched — construction, leisure and hospitality, education and health — are growing 1.27%. Naming the moving sides matters, because it is what rules out a general slump: in an ordinary downturn both sides fall together, and the hands-on side is adding jobs at a healthy clip. The bond market is not pricing a recession either; the yield curve is positive rather than inverted.

But this panel cannot carry the reading by itself, and I want to be exact about why. A widening gap between exposed and control industries is precisely what perfect reallocation would look like. If everyone who left an information-sector job walked into a health-care job, the exposed side would fall, the control side would rise, and the gap would open — with nobody worse off. Control industries growing at 1.27% is arithmetically consistent with them absorbing the entire outflow. The gap tells you something is specific to AI-exposed work. It does not tell you the people are stranded.

The gap has also stopped widening. It stood at -2.61 last month and -2.54 now, roughly flat across the last four readings. A gap that sits still is a standing condition, not news.

The 2021-22 hiring correction, weighed against the reading

Information and professional services over-hired badly in 2021-22 and have been unwinding ever since. This predates the current generation of AI tools, and I weigh it against the displacement reading rather than alongside it. It plausibly explains a large share of the exposed employment decline. It explains why the gap in job postings opened in 2022, which lines up with the interest-rate shock rather than with any model release. It explains much of the level of today's gap.

What it does not explain is the residual, and the residual is the reading. The correction is now roughly four years old and should be decaying, yet exposed industries are still contracting in absolute terms in mid-2026 while the rest of the economy adds jobs. And a hiring hangover in two sectors does not obviously produce a 1.4-million fall in prime-age employment across the whole economy or a four-point rise in long-term unemployment. That leftover is thin, and it is what I am calling displacement.

The absorption panel, and the honest case against it

The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months. Two things make that reading better than it sounds and one makes it worse.

Better: the level is still 0.25 points above where it stood in 2019. This is not a collapse; it is a good market getting less good. And the fall is not a statistical artifact of a growing population — the count of employed people itself fell by 1.44 million, so the ratio is falling because the numerator dropped.

Worse: the whole twelve-month decline happened inside the last three months. That is one quarter of evidence presented as a year of evidence. It comes from the household survey, which has had documented response problems through this period, and 2026 also carried a large one-off population revision in January. A single noisy quarter in this survey is a completely ordinary thing to see. If I am wrong about displacement, this is most likely where I am wrong, and I cannot rule it out from inside the data.

The supporting detail around it splits. Long-term unemployment at 27.3% is high in level terms and up 4.0 points over the year, but this series is genuinely volatile and a move of that size is suggestive rather than decisive. The broader underemployment measure has widened very slightly. Against that, layoffs are low at 1.1% of employment and still falling, and hiring minus quits sits on the comfortable side. Read together, low layoffs and weak hiring describe a frozen market, not a shedding one. Incumbents are not being pushed out. The pain is falling on people trying to get in — new entrants and people already unemployed. That is compatible with AI displacing work through simply not replacing leavers, which is what I think is going on if this reading is right. It is equally compatible with an ordinary late-cycle hiring freeze that has nothing to do with AI. I cannot separate those two from here.

The strongest thing arguing against displacement

Job postings. Advertised openings for knowledge work sit 23.1% below their February 2020 level, while postings for hands-on work sit 5.3% above theirs. That is a large gap and it looks damning until you read the direction: over the last six months the knowledge-work side has been recovering, closing about 2.6 points of the gap. The level is largely a 2022 interest-rate event still sitting in the data; the change is the news, and the change is on the improving side.

This cuts hard against the displacement reading for two reasons. Postings lead actual hiring, so this panel should turn before the employment numbers do. And it is cut by type of work rather than by industry, which is a better way of identifying who is actually exposed to AI than counting everyone employed in the information sector, janitors included. So the indicator most likely to be right first, on the better measure of exposure, says demand for exposed work is stabilising or slightly improving. It is also fresher — July, against June for everything supporting the displacement reading. The counter-signal is not stale; the supporting evidence is the older material. This is the single biggest reason the reading is low confidence rather than moderate.

I am not treating strong hands-on postings as evidence of absorption. Demand rotating between kinds of work is not the same as workers rotating with it, and a job advertisement is an advertised intention, not a hire.

Pay, and why I am not using it

Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing 4.63% a year against 3.53% in barely-touched industries, and that gap widened this month. On its face that is backwards from displacement. I am not counting it for either side, because there is a mechanical explanation that fits too well. Employment in those industries is falling. If junior hiring in information and professional services has stopped, the people left are more senior on average, and the average wage rises with nobody getting a raise.

The check on this points the same way. A separate measure that follows the same individuals twelve months apart shows people who stayed in their jobs getting 3.6% and people who switched getting 4.4%, neither accelerating, while the industry average jumped four-tenths of a point in a single month. Averages moving when the people underneath them change is exactly what that pattern looks like. The pay panel is unresolved, not supportive.

That same individual-level tracker does carry one genuine piece of counter-evidence: job switchers are still being paid a premium of about 0.8 points over stayers, and that premium has been recovering. People who move are being bid for. Two limits on it. It is economy-wide, covering every worker in the country, so it cannot say anything specific about workers leaving AI-exposed jobs — a different and much smaller group. And it is a median, so a bad outcome concentrated in a minority is precisely the shape it would miss.

Productivity

Output per hour is running at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, and briefly inside the band the late-1990s internet boom produced. If AI were making workers more valuable rather than redundant, gains showing up in productivity is what that would look like, and this is the most substantive point on the augmentation side of the board. Three things hold me back from leaning on it. It is economy-wide and cannot attribute anything to AI-exposed work. It is measured through March 2026, a quarter older than the jobs and employment figures, so it cannot yet reflect a turn in either direction. And output per hour rises arithmetically when hours fall faster than output — which is also what a displacement episode produces. One good quarter is not a break in trend.

Worth noting alongside it: labor's share of national income is 51.0% and has fallen four quarters running, now below its previous record low. That share has been drifting down for forty years for reasons that have nothing to do with AI, and it typically drops in recessions, so I count it as zero evidence. It is evocative rather than probative — productivity elevated while labor's slice shrinks unusually fast is the shape gains not reaching workers would take.

Alternatives I considered and rejected

A general recession. Fails immediately: the un-exposed side of the economy is adding jobs at 1.27% a year and its postings are above pre-pandemic levels. A general slump pulls both sides down.

The 2022 interest-rate shock as the whole story. This is the strongest rival and I gave it real weight, as described above. It explains the level of the postings gap and much of the exposed jobs decline. It does not explain why prime-age employment is falling now, in mid-2026, with the yield curve positive and the untouched industries growing. Mixed evidence is not the same as a confounded reading, so I did not convert it into a non-answer.

Augmentation. The affirmative case would need productivity gains plus pay rising for exposed workers. The pay leg is disqualified by the composition problem above and contradicted by the individual-level tracker. That leaves an economy-wide productivity number five months old with one quarter inside its band. Augmentation working would need positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, and there is no composition-proof, exposed-industry version of that anywhere in this data. So augmentation would have to rest on the absence of anything bad happening — and something bad is happening in the employment numbers, so it cannot rest even there.

News

Coverage of the Iran conflict is too recent to be in June data, and a war-driven demand shock would hit construction and hospitality at least as hard as information and professional services, which is the opposite of the pattern here. Federal Reserve and mortgage coverage is the live version of the interest-rate story and is already discounted in how I read the postings panel. The monthly payrolls report showed 158,984,000 jobs, up 57,000, with unemployment at 4.2% — economy-wide, from the establishment survey, so it cannot speak to exposed industries specifically and cannot be netted against the household survey's prime-age figure. What it does do is make the "untouched industries are booming and absorbing everyone" story less comfortable than the 1.27% growth figure alone suggests: total hiring across the economy is barely positive. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York piece attributing hiring weakness to AI is a hypothesis to test against the series, not corroboration of them, and it generated no test I was not already running.

What would show this reading is wrong

If the prime-age employment rate stops falling year on year — the twelve-month change coming back to -0.1 or better — while the exposed-versus-control jobs gap also pulls back to -2.2 or narrower, then the people leaving exposed work were being absorbed all along and the last quarter was noise. Both series publish monthly and will produce two or three new readings before early November, so this will get tested. What would push the reading the other way, toward higher confidence in displacement, is the knowledge-work postings gap resuming its widening, or a second consecutive quarter of falling prime-age employment confirming that the last one was real.
